about: THE SEVEN AGES, 793-1066. How the merchant's world changes while the house goes on through its heirs. One entry an age: from/to (years), name (plain), world (what the world is like for a merchant), rulers (who rules where, with dates; 'realm' is an id from ports_793.json where one fits, else empty), trade (what is traded differently and why), goods (ids from goods_793.json: more = wanted or carried more than before, less = scarcer or fading), danger, new (ships, coins, towns, laws and other things that appear, each with its year and source), gone (what ends), ports (ids from ports_793.json that rise or fall in the age; 'lacking' names places the table does not have yet), stories (three true stories of the age a merchant would hear, each with its source; 'chronicle' is the id of the matching entry in chronicle_793.json where there is one), sources. Words are our own; the few quoted lines are from public-domain translations and say so. All dates Julian. (?) marks what could not be checked. Abbreviations: ARF Annales regni Francorum, AB Annals of St-Bertin, AF Annals of Fulda, AX Annals of Xanten, ASC Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (its year first, the true year after '='), AU Annals of Ulster, PVL the Russian Primary Chronicle, MGH Monumenta Germaniae Historica. Written 4 October 2026 as a draft for the user to overwrite. Design notes: Design/ages.md.

ages.name: The emperor's peace
ages.world: One ruler holds the land from the Pyrenees to the Elbe, and his peace, his penny and his toll-men reach every river mouth a Frisian uses. Dorestat is the greatest market of the north. Frisian skippers carry Rhine wine, querns and cloth to the English wics, to Ripa and on into the Baltic. The Northmen are neighbours and customers first: their raids fall on islands and minsters at the edges (Lindisfarne 793, Iona 795, Herio 799) and once, in 810, on the Frisian islands. The Saxon war ends in 804 and the border with the Danes is sworn on the Eider in 811. The English are four or five kingdoms, with Mercia on top until 825 and Wessex after.

ages.trade: Wine, querns of Mayen lava, Badorf pots, glass and sword blades go down the Rhine; Frisian cloth, salt and grain go with them; furs, amber, wax, walrus ivory and captives come back from the north and east. In Francia and England a penny is counted. North of the Eider silver is weighed, and from about 800 more and more of it is the caliph's dirhams, come up the Russian rivers. The emperor makes the rules of the market: one heavy penny that no one may refuse (794), fixed grain prices in a famine (794, 806), no byrnies or swords sold out of the realm (803, 805), no new tolls (805), a top price on cloaks (808). His tenth is taken at Dorestat and at Quentovic. The English send cloaks and ask for 'black stones', and two kings write a treaty about merchants (796).
ages.danger: Weather, shoals and the toll-man. The sea is safer now than it will be for two hundred years. Famine (793, 805-806), the cattle plague of 809-810 and hard winters (810, 813, 821) move prices more than any raider. Raiders are few and far off: three ships, a dozen, and they go for islands and minsters. The one war a Frisian feels is the Danish border: Godfred's 200 ships on the Frisian islands in 810, and 100 pounds of silver paid. From 830 the emperor's sons rise against him and the coast guard is left to rot.

stories.title: The king's letter about cloaks
stories.text: Some years back Charles and Offa of Mercia fell out over a marriage, and each closed his ports to the other's ships. Now Charles has written to make it up. Pilgrims are to pass free. Men who slip in among them to trade must pay toll at the proper places. Merchants of either realm are to have the other king's protection and may come before him if they are wronged. Offa asked for 'black stones': let him send a man to say what kind, and they will be found and helped on their way. And Charles asks one thing back: that the English make their cloaks as long as they used to.
stories.source: Charles to Offa, 796: MGH Epistolae IV, Alcuini Epistolae no. 100. The closed ports, about 790: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium 12.2; Alcuin, Ep. 7.

stories.title: Godfred moves a market
stories.text: Godfred, king of the Danes, fell on the Obodrites, the emperor's friends. Before he went home he destroyed their trading place on the coast, which the Danes call Reric and which paid his kingdom a great deal in tolls. He put its merchants aboard his ships and landed them at Sliesthorp. Then he had a rampart built across the neck of Jutland from the eastern sea to the western, with one gate in it for carts and riders. A man with partners at Reric must look for them now at the head of the Schlei.
stories.source: ARF 808

stories.title: Forty books lost
stories.text: The monk Ansgar sailed for Birka in a company of merchants, with the emperor's gifts for the king of the Svear. About halfway pirates fell on them. The merchants fought and won the first bout, lost the second, and lost their ships and all their goods. The monks lost the royal gifts and nearly forty books. They went on by land, a very long way on foot, crossing the waters between by boat, and came to Birka. King Björn let them preach, and the town's reeve, Herigar, built a church on his own ground.
stories.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 10-11 (read in C. H. Robinson's translation, 1921)

ages.name: The raiding years
ages.world: The emperor's sons fight him and then each other (Fontenoy, 841), and at Verdun in 843 the empire is cut in three. Frisia and the Rhine mouths fall to Lothar's middle kingdom. The Northmen learn of it at once. Dorestat is sacked in 834, 835, 836 and 837, and again in 846, 847, 857 and 863. Fleets go up the Seine, the Loire, the Thames and the Rhine, and from 843 they winter where they raid. Kings answer with silver (Paris, 845: 7,000 pounds) or by giving a river mouth to one Dane to hold against the others: Walcheren to Harald (841), Dorestat to Rorik (850). For the north the same years are good ones: Sliesthorp, Ripa and Birka get churches and a share of Dorestat's trade.

ages.trade: The goods are the old ones; the middlemen change. Dorestat's Frisians trade on under a Danish lord, then move upriver and east: to Deventer, to Tiel on the Waal, to Cologne, to Sliesthorp, where merchants from Dorestat are seen about 850. Loot, ransom and captives become goods like any other. A fleet in winter camp is a market: it sells church plate, books and people and buys bread, wine, horses and arms, and in 864 the western king makes selling it a horse or a byrnie a death matter. An abbot's ransom is 686 pounds of gold and 3,250 of silver (Saint-Denis, 858). Silver runs north as tribute and is weighed out again in the Baltic. Salt and wine from the Loire grow dear while the Northmen sit on Herio (from 843). The western king's pennies get worse year by year until 864, when all are called in and struck new at ten mints.
ages.danger: Every river mouth from the Elbe to the Garonne is raided, most summers, and nobody knows which one this year. Fleets grow from a dozen ships to 120 (the Seine, 845) and 350 (the Thames, 851). A winter camp on an island closes a river for years: Herio from 843, Thanet 851, Sheppey 855, Oissel in the Seine 856-861. The kings fight each other harder than they fight the fleets. And the sea kills more at one blow than any fleet: the flood of 26 December 838 drowns 2,437 in Frisia. The winter of 859-860 is the hardest anyone remembers.

stories.title: Two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven
stories.text: On the day after Christmas the sea came over Frisia, far past any tide men knew. It lay over nearly the whole land, as high as the dunes. Whatever it rolled across it took: people, beasts and houses alike. Afterwards the dead were counted with great care, and the count came to 2,437. The bishop who wrote the year down at the emperor's court gave the number as it was reported to him.
stories.source: AB 839 (the flood of 26 December 838), written by Prudentius of Troyes

stories.title: Easter in Paris
stories.text: A fleet of 120 ships under a chief the Franks call Ragnar came up the Seine in March. King Charles set his army on both banks. The Northmen beat the smaller half and hanged 111 prisoners in sight of the other. They came into Paris on Easter Sunday and found it empty. Charles paid them 7,000 pounds of silver to go. On the way home a sickness ran through the fleet. At King Horik's court Ragnar boasted of the silver and the empty city, and died soon after of the same sickness, so the monks of Saint-Germain heard; and Horik, afraid, offered to give the captives back.
stories.source: AB 845; AX 845; Translatio sancti Germani Parisiensis (about 850). The hanging and Ragnar's death are from the Translatio (?)

stories.title: The toll goes to a Dane
stories.text: Rorik the Dane held Dorestat once before with his brother, under the old emperor. He fell out with Lothar, fled to the Saxons, gathered ships and came back raiding the coast he knew. He took Dorestat. Lothar could not drive him out without harm to his own people, so he took him back as his man on terms: Rorik holds Dorestat and the counties about it, gathers the king's taxes and dues faithfully, and keeps off the Danish pirates. A Frisian now pays the king's toll to a Dane, and is safer for it.
stories.source: AF 850 (the fullest account); AB 850; AX 850

ages.name: The great armies
ages.world: The raiders stop going home. A great army lands in East Anglia in 865 and in thirteen years ends three English kingdoms: Northumbria (867), East Anglia (869) and Mercia (874). Only Alfred's Wessex holds (Edington, 878). The army shares out the land and ploughs it (876-880), and York, Lincoln and the towns of the Danish midlands become places that trade. From 879 another army works the Scheldt, Meuse, Rhine and Seine: it burns Cologne and stables its horses in the chapel at Aachen (881), takes Frisia as a fief (882-885), besieges Paris (885-886) and is broken on the Dyle (891). The Frankish empire comes apart for good in 887-888. Far off, the same people settle Iceland (from about 870) and take Kiev (882). Dorestat is a village; the Rhine trade passes through Tiel, Deventer and Cologne.

ages.trade: An army is the biggest customer on the coast. It sells captives, plate and cattle and buys horses, corn, wine and arms, tens of pounds of silver at a time; where it settles, it wants what any farmer wants. Two ways of paying now live side by side: counted pennies in Wessex and Francia, weighed silver in the Danish lands (cut coin, rings and bars, small folding scales and cube weights), and a merchant needs both skills. Kings pull trade inside walls: Alfred's fortified towns, London moved inside the Roman wall (886), the ring forts of Flanders and Zeeland, Deventer's earth wall after 882. Godfrid the Dane, given Frisia, asks for Koblenz, Andernach and Sinzig as well, because his own land grows no wine. Ohthere brings the far north to market: walrus ivory, walrus-hide rope, furs, down. Iceland opens, a land with no timber, corn or good iron of its own. Frisians serve as Alfred's shipmen (896) as well as trading.
ages.danger: Armies of thousands, on horses, that winter in the land: Thetford, Repton, Ghent, Elsloo, Leuven. A kingdom can change lords within one sailing season, and a charter from a dead king is worth nothing. The Rhine and Meuse are raided far inland in 881-882; Frisia is a Danish duchy for three years. On the English coast Alfred's ships and the Danes' fight in the river mouths (896). After 891 the armies thin out, and the last years bring a worse killer: three years of cattle plague and sickness in England (893-896).

stories.title: Tribute refused
stories.text: Rodulf, a Dane of the royal kin who had plundered on both sides of the sea, came with his ships into Oostergo and sent to the Frisians for tribute. They answered that they owed tribute to King Louis and his sons and to no one else. He landed. A Northman who had been baptised and had lived long among the Frisians led them out against him. Rodulf fell first, and eight hundred with him; the western annals say five hundred. The rest shut themselves in a building. The same Northman talked the Frisians out of storming it: it was God's strength and not ours that won this, he said, so take hostages and let them buy their lives. The Danes sent back a great treasure from their ships and swore never to come again.
stories.source: AF 873; AB 873; AX 873 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodulf_Haraldsson, checked 4 October 2026)

stories.title: The man who lived furthest north
stories.text: Ohthere told his lord King Alfred that he lived furthest north of all Northmen. Once he sailed north along the land to see how far it went: three days to where the whale hunters turn back, three days more, then east and south round the land to a great river where the Beormas live. He went for the walrus too, whose teeth are fine bone and whose hide makes the best ship rope. He was among the first men of his country, yet he had only twenty cattle, twenty sheep and twenty swine, and ploughed a little with horses. His wealth was six hundred tame reindeer and what the Finnas paid him in skins, down, whalebone and rope. From his home he sailed south more than a month to the port of Sciringes heal, and from there five days to Hedeby.
stories.source: The Old English Orosius I.1, about 890 (our own words; public-domain translations: Thorpe 1853, Sweet 1883)

stories.title: A boat without oars
stories.text: Three Irishmen came ashore in Cornwall in a boat made of two and a half hides, with no oars and food for seven nights. On the seventh night they reached land. They had stolen away from Ireland because they wished for the love of God to be on pilgrimage and did not care where. They went straight to King Alfred. Their names were Dubslane, Macbeth and Maelinmun. The Chronicle: 'And three Scots came to King Alfred in a boat without any oars from Ireland; whence they stole away, because they would live in a state of pilgrimage, for the love of God, they recked not where.'
stories.source: ASC 891, tr. J. Ingram 1823 (https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp); 'Scots' is the Chronicle's word for the Irish

ages.name: Walled towns and eastern silver
ages.world: The raiders' grandsons are lords and townsmen. Rollo holds Rouen from the western king (911). Danish kings, then Dublin's Northmen, hold York until 954. Dublin itself, lost in 902, is founded again in 917 with Waterford and Limerick beside it. Against them Edward the Elder and his sister Æthelflæd wall town after town and take back the Danish midlands (910-918); Æthelstan takes York (927), wins at Brunanburh (937) and calls himself king of all Britain. East of the Rhine the Saxon kings Henry and Otto wall their towns against the Magyars and make the Danes at Sliesthorp pay tribute (934). The great business of the age comes from the east: Samanid silver flows up the Volga, and Birka, Gotland, Sliesthorp, York and Dublin all live on it. Tiel and Deventer are the Frisians' markets, and about 920 the bishop comes home to Utrecht.

ages.trade: Kings now say where trade may happen. Edward's law: buy in a town, before the town-reeve. Æthelstan's at Grately (about 928): nothing worth over 20 pence bought outside a town, one coinage for the whole realm, moneyers named town by town (London eight, Canterbury seven, Winchester six, Southampton two). So markets, mints and tolls gather inside the new walls: London, Winchester, Chester, York, Lincoln, Norwich; Rouen under its Northmen; Cologne, Mainz, Tiel, Deventer. Silver is plentiful. Dirhams struck at Samarkand and Tashkent pass the Bulghars' market on the Volga, Ladoga, Birka and Gotland and end as rings and cut pieces in English and Irish hoards (Cuerdale, about 905). They are paid for in furs, wax, honey and captives; Dublin and Rouen are the west's markets for people. On the Rhine the hard painted pots of Pingsdorf replace Badorf's about 900. Norway sells whetstones and soapstone, Iceland its wadmal. Cargo ships built to sail, with few oars, appear (Äskekärr: 16 m, 20 tons).
ages.danger: Less at sea than before, more on land. The Magyars ride through Saxony, Lotharingia and Burgundy again and again from 900 to 955, and a walled town is the only safe night. The war for York (919-954) makes the Humber, the Irish Sea and the road between Dublin and York dangerous by turns. Brittany and the Loire are in the Northmen's hands from 919 to 936. Fleets from Brittany and Dublin raid the Severn and Wales (914). A dimmed sun in 939 is followed by hard winters and hunger in Ireland and Germany (?).

new.what: Pingsdorf ware: hard, pale, red-painted pots from the Rhineland, in place of Badorf's.

The Äskekärr ship built on the Göta river: 16 m long, 4.6 m broad, about 20 tons of cargo, open hold amidships; repaired as late as about 1010.
Rouen and the lower Seine granted to Rollo: Normandy.

The Northmen's hold on Brittany: Alan comes back from England and retakes Nantes (937).

stories.title: Forty pounds for a bishop
stories.text: A great fleet came north from Brittany under two earls, Ohter and Hroald, and went round west into the mouth of the Severn. It raided the Welsh coast wherever it liked and took Cyfeiliog, bishop in Archenfield, down to the ships. King Edward bought him back for forty pounds. Then the men of Hereford and Gloucester beat the raiders in the field, and the king set a watch along the whole south shore of the Severn sea. The fleet sat on an island in the channel until many starved. What was left went to Dyfed and from there to Ireland in the autumn.
stories.source: ASC (A) 917, (D) 915 (= 914); Ingram 1823 prints it under 918

stories.title: The merchants at the wooden post
stories.text: The caliph's envoy watched the Rus traders camped by the Volga at the Bulghar king's market. He had never seen bodies more perfect, he wrote: tall as palm trees, fair and ruddy. Each man kept an axe, a sword and a knife by him always. A wife wore a neck ring for every ten thousand dirhams her husband owned, and green glass beads bought at a dirham each. When a ship came in, her master went to a tall wooden post with bread, meat, onions, milk and drink, told it how many girls and sable skins he had brought, and asked it for a merchant with many dinars and dirhams who would buy what he was offered and not argue.
stories.source: Ibn Fadlan, Risala (922), the account of the Rusiyyah (our own words)

stories.title: The great fight
stories.text: Olaf Guthfrithson, king of Dublin, brought a fleet into England to win York, with Constantine king of Scots and the king of the Strathclyde Britons beside him. Æthelstan and his brother Edmund met them at Brunanburh and fought from sunrise to dark. Five young kings lay dead on the field and seven of Olaf's earls, and Constantine's son. Olaf was driven to his ship with few men and went back over deep water to Dublin. The English made a song of it, and the song says no greater slaughter was seen in the island since the Angles and Saxons first came over the broad sea.
stories.source: ASC (A) 937, the poem; AU 937

ages.name: The quiet years
ages.world: For one long generation nobody burns a port. Otto breaks the Magyars on the Lech (955) and is crowned emperor (962). Edgar rules all England in peace (959-975). Harald Bluetooth makes the Danes one kingdom and Christian (about 965) and builds his ring forts (980). Towns fill: London, Winchester, York, Cologne, Tiel, Rouen, Ghent. Then the eastern silver stops. The mines fail, the Rus break the Khazars (965-969), and Birka is given up about 975 while a king's town, Sigtuna, takes its place. New silver comes out of the Harz from about 968 and goes north as German pennies. From 980 strange sails are seen off the English coast again.

rulers.who: Eadwig, Edgar, Edward 'the Martyr', Æthelred II

rulers.where: The German kingdom and the empire, with Frisia and the Rhine
rulers.who: Otto I, Otto II, Otto III

ages.trade: The money changes. Dirhams thin out after about 950 and are gone from the west by the 970s. In their place come German pennies and English ones. Edgar's reform (about 973) makes one design of penny for all England, struck in some forty towns and called in every few years: a stranger must change his silver at the mint and lose a little each time. Edgar also sets one weight and one measure, London's and Winchester's, and a price for wool: 120 pence the wey. The emperor grants market, mint and toll to bishops (Bremen 965, Magdeburg 965), and the bishop's toll-man replaces the count's. Tiel is one of the four great toll places of the German kingdom, with Mainz, Cologne and Bardowick (975). Merchants of Cologne and Tiel are regular in London, and Flemish towns begin to weave English wool. At Mainz in 965 a traveller from Spain sees dirhams of Samarkand, and pepper, ginger and cloves. With no war to feed it, the trade in captives shrinks in the west and moves east, to Prague and the Rus rivers.
ages.danger: Little, and that is the point: these are the years to build. The risks are a toll-man's, a moneyer's and a bishop's court's. Towns burn and sicken (London, 962); there is famine in England in 976 and a cattle plague in 986. On the Danish border Otto II storms the Danevirke (974) and the Danes take it back (983), the year the Slavs rise and burn Hamburg. From 980 small fleets, seven ships at a time, fall on Southampton, Thanet and Cheshire (980), Padstow (981), Portland (982) and Watchet (988).

The Danes' king baptised; the great rune stone at Jelling says he 'made the Danes Christian'.
Market, mint and toll at Bremen granted to the archbishop, with the king's peace on its merchants; the same at Magdeburg.

stories.title: The hot iron
stories.text: At a feast before King Harald the Danes argued about gods. They granted that Christ was a god, but said there were others greater, who showed men stronger signs. A priest named Poppo answered that there was one God only and the rest were demons. The king, a man quick to listen and slow to speak, asked whether he would prove it on his own body. Next morning the king had a great weight of iron heated, and Poppo carried it as far as he was told and showed his hand unhurt. Then the king ordered that Christ alone be honoured in his kingdom.
stories.source: Widukind of Corvey, Res gestae Saxonicae III.65 (written about 968)

stories.title: Kings at the oars
stories.text: After he was crowned at Bath at Pentecost, King Edgar took his whole fleet round Wales to Chester. Six kings came to meet him there and swore to be his helpers by sea and by land. Men told it bigger afterwards: eight kings, they said, among them the king of Scots, the king of the Cumbrians and Maccus, king of many islands, and they rowed Edgar on the Dee from his hall to the church of Saint John while he held the steering oar.
stories.source: ASC (D, E) 973 for the six kings and the oath; the eight kings and the rowing are from John of Worcester, Chronicle under 973 (written about 1120-1140)

stories.title: A good name for a land
stories.text: Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland for killings, spent three winters finding out a land in the west. He called it Greenland, because, he said, men would be keener to go there if it had a good name. The summer he went back to settle it, twenty-five ships sailed with him from Breiðafjörður and Borgarfjörður. Fourteen arrived. Some were driven back and some were lost.
stories.source: Ari, Íslendingabók 6 (the name and the date: fourteen or fifteen winters before Iceland took the faith); Landnámabók for the ships

ages.name: Tribute, then one king
ages.world: The fleets come back to England, bigger and led by kings, and Æthelred buys them off: 10,000 pounds in 991, 16,000 in 994, 24,000 in 1002, 36,000 in 1007, 48,000 in 1012. The silver goes home with the crews and lies in every northern hoard. Sweyn Forkbeard takes England in 1013. His son Cnut holds it from 1016, Denmark from 1018 and Norway from 1028, and for twenty years one king's peace covers the North Sea. Tolls on the roads to Rome are lowered (1027) and the biggest cargo ships of the age are built. The north is baptised: Norway under two Olafs, Iceland by a vote (1000), the king of the Svear at Sigtuna. On the Rhine mouths Tiel is burned (1006) and rebuilt, and the count of West Frisia sets a toll at Vlaardingen and beats the emperor's army to keep it (1018). Cnut dies in 1035 and his sons cannot hold three kingdoms.

the lawspeaker Thorgeir decides for baptism in 1000

ages.trade: English pennies are the north's money. More of Æthelred's coins have been found in Scandinavia than in England, and the kings there copy them: at Sigtuna (about 995), at Dublin (997), then in Denmark and Norway. The last dirhams reach the Baltic in the 1010s. London is the chief port of the north. Its toll list, of about 1000, names men of Rouen with wine and blubber-fish, men of Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and France, men of Huy, Liège and Nivelles, and the emperor's men, who may trade like Londoners and pay at Christmas and Easter in cloth, pepper, gloves and vinegar. The merchants of Tiel sail to England as a sworn fellowship with their own law. A Frisians' guild raises rune stones at Sigtuna. Bruges is praised for its crowd of merchants (1037). From the far west come walrus ivory and falcons, from Norway dried fish. Captives are still sold through Dublin, and the archbishop of York preaches against it (1014).
ages.danger: Until 1016 England is the most dangerous coast on the chart: fleets of ninety ships and more every few years, towns burned from Ipswich (991) to Exeter (1003), Norwich and Thetford (1004), Oxford (1010) and Canterbury (1011). The king answers with a massacre (Saint Brice's Day, 1002) and with tribute. The Rhine mouths are struck in 1006 and 1007, Stavoren in 991, Stade in 994. The sea takes its share: the flood of Michaelmas eve, 1014. Famine in 1005, such as no one remembered. Then Cnut pays off the fleet (1018), and for twenty years the worst a merchant meets between the Thames and the Sound is a toll. War comes back only at the edges: Olaf of Norway and the Svear king against Cnut (1026), and Wendish raiders in the Danish straits once Cnut is dead.

stories.title: Wine from the south
stories.text: The army that took Canterbury held Archbishop Ælfheah for seven months, waiting for his ransom, and he forbade anyone to pay it. On the Saturday after Easter, at Greenwich, they were very drunk, for wine had been brought to them from the south. They led him to their meeting and killed him there. The Chronicle: 'They overwhelmed him with bones and horns of oxen; and one of them smote him with an axe-iron on the head.' The tribute, 48,000 pounds, was paid all the same. Then Thorkell went over to King Æthelred with forty-five ships.
stories.source: ASC 1012, tr. J. Ingram 1823 (https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang11.asp); Thietmar of Merseburg VII.42-43

stories.title: What a monk thought of Tiel
stories.text: A monk of the bishopric of Utrecht wrote down what he thought of the merchants of Tiel. They are hard men, used to no discipline. They judge their cases by their own will and not by the law, and say the emperor gave them a charter for it. A debt denied on oath is a debt cancelled, so they swear easily. They start drinking early in the morning, and the man who tells the coarsest joke in the loudest voice gets the praise. They put their money together and share it out for feasts at set times of the year. And when the count set his toll at Vlaardingen, these were the men who told the emperor that unless he acted they could no longer sail to the island of Britain, nor the Britons come to them, and his own tolls would be the poorer.
stories.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20-21, written about 1021-1024 (MGH SS 4; ed. H. van Rij 1980); our own words

stories.title: The king's letter from Rome
stories.text: Cnut went to Rome for the emperor's crowning and wrote home to all his people. He had spoken, he said, with the emperor, the pope and the princes there about the needs of the English and the Danes: that they should have fairer law and safer peace on the road to Rome, and not be stopped at so many barriers or worn down by unjust tolls. The emperor agreed, and King Rudolf, who holds most of the barriers in the passes, and all the princes sealed it: his people, merchants and those who travel to pray alike, may go and come back in firm peace and under just law.
stories.source: Cnut's letter of 1027, kept in John of Worcester's Chronicle (under 1031) and William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.183; our own words

ages.name: The last years
ages.world: Cnut's sea-kingdom is gone and three houses want its pieces. Edward, Æthelred's son, comes home from Normandy to be king of the English (1042). Magnus of Norway holds Denmark too until 1047; then Harald of Norway and Sweyn of Denmark fight for seventeen summers, and Sliesthorp is burned in one of them (1050). In England the house of Godwine grows greater than the king. In Normandy Duke William grows up, wins his battles and builds castles. Flanders under Baldwin V is rich on cloth and on being everyone's refuge. In Frisia the counts strike their own pennies, and the count of West Frisia is killed at Dordrecht (1049). Edward dies on 5 January 1066. A long-haired star is seen after Easter. By Christmas Harald of Norway and Harold of England are dead and William is crowned at Westminster.

ages.trade: The pattern of the next three hundred years is already here: English wool to Flemish looms, Flemish cloth everywhere, wine from Rouen and the Rhine to London, German silver to pay for it. Bruges is a port; Ghent and Saint-Omer weave. London, Winchester, York, Lincoln and Norwich are towns of thousands. Edward ends the army-tax and pays off the last hired ships (1050-1051); instead the Kentish ports owe ship service for their freedoms (Dover: twenty ships for fifteen days, twenty-one men in each). The Frisians' own counts strike pennies at Dokkum, Leeuwarden, Stavoren and Bolsward. Harald's Norwegian pennies are poor silver: take them by weight. After 1050 Sliesthorp's trade crosses the fjord to Schleswig. The north sells dried fish, ivory, furs and falcons. In a bad year grain is the cargo: wheat at sixty pence the sester in 1044.
ages.danger: A war every summer somewhere. Norway against Denmark in the Danish straits (1048-1064); Wends on the Jutland coast (1043); the emperor against Flanders, with Edward's fleet lying at Sandwich to shut the sea (1049); Godwine's ships against the king (1052); Welsh and Irish fleets in the Severn (1049, 1055, 1058). Small fleets still raid and sell: twenty-five ships take men, gold and silver at Sandwich in 1048 and sell them in Flanders. A hard winter (1046-1047), famine (1044), cattle sickness (1054). And in 1066 every ship on the south and east coasts is called out or seized: Tostig in May, Harald's three hundred in September, William's fleet out of Saint-Valery on the night of 27 September.

stories.title: Sixty pence the sester
stories.text: There was very great hunger over all England, and corn dearer than anyone remembered. The Chronicle gives the price as a merchant would: 'the sester of wheat rose to sixty pence, and even further.' The same year the king went out to Sandwich with thirty-five ships. A man with a hold of Rhineland or Frankish grain could have named his own price.
stories.source: ASC 1044 (E under 1043), tr. J. Ingram 1823 (https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang11.asp); the last sentence is ours

stories.title: Burned from end to end
stories.text: In the war for Denmark, Harald of Norway sailed into the Schlei and burned Sliesthorp from end to end. One of his men made a verse of it: he stood on the town's rampart before dawn and watched the flames climb from the houses, and reckoned it a deed that would hurt Sweyn. A priest of Bremen wrote that ships used to sail from that harbour to the Slav lands, to Sweden, to Samland and as far as Greece. Sixteen years later the Slavs finished what was left, and the townsmen moved across the water to Schleswig.
stories.source: Snorri, Heimskringla, Haralds saga Sigurðarsonar 34, with the verses of Harald's men (written about 1230 from 11th-century verse); Adam of Bremen IV.1 and III.51

stories.title: The long-haired star
stories.text: On the eve of the Greater Litany, the twenty-fourth of April, a star with a long tail was seen over all England, and it shone for a week. Soon after, Earl Tostig came raiding with as many ships as he could get. In September Harald of Norway came into the Humber with three hundred ships. He and Tostig beat the northern earls outside York, and five days later King Harold killed them both at Stamford Bridge. Twenty-four ships were enough to carry the Norwegians home. Three days after that Duke William landed at Pevensey. A merchant in Flanders or on the Rhine heard these things in the order the ships brought them, and not always the right way round.
stories.source: ASC (C, D, E) 1066; the last sentence is ours
